source: Kim et al. (2026) Multi-Agent Transactive Memory
finding: Names a shared repository of agent trajectories 'transactive memory' after Wegner. Consumer agents retrieve successful 5-step action chunks keyed by task plus recent history. Retrieval beat no retrieval on both benchmarks.
numbers: ALFWorld success 47.1% to 55.1% (single-stage dense retrieval), steps 11.77 to 11.18. WebArena 18.2% to 20.5%, steps 21.99 to 20.26. 34-model population; E5-Base embedder; top-20 then top-1 rerank; mean of 5 runs.
limits: Only successful trajectories indexed. Two benchmarks. Rerankers trained and tested inside one benchmark. No adversarial producers. It borrows only the name: there is no 'who knows what' directory of agents, only a shared pool.
agent_relevance: Shows a shared experience store helps. But the real TMS element (directory of expertise, credibility) is absent; our design must decide if it needs one.

source: Kim et al. (2026) Multi-Agent Transactive Memory: learning-to-rank reranker
finding: A small learned reranker over retrieved trajectories added more gain on ALFWorld than plain retrieval. Gains on WebArena were smaller and reranker-specific.
numbers: ALFWorld success: no retrieval 0.4708, single 0.5511, FFN 0.5861, LambdaMART 0.5715, SVMRank 0.6431; steps 10.35 for SVMRank. WebArena 0.1818 / 0.2045 / 0.2045 / 0.1818 / 0.2045. LambdaMART fell back to the no-retrieval success rate on WebArena.
limits: Reranker features fit ALFWorld task structure; weak transfer to WebArena (47 tasks in the ablation, so one task is about 2 points).
agent_relevance: Retrieval quality, not just having a store, drives the gain. A selection step (who or what to consult) matters.

source: Kim et al. (2026) Multi-Agent Transactive Memory: scope ablation and oracle ceiling
finding: Allowing any trajectory beat restricting to same-task-type or cross-task-type pools. Even trajectories from other task types helped. An exact-match trajectory is a big ceiling.
numbers: ALFWorld (274 tasks) SR full 0.646, same type 0.631, cross type 0.599. WebArena (47 tasks) 0.298 / 0.277 / 0.192. Oracle exact-task trajectories: ALFWorld 20.07 to 38.69, WebArena 16.58 to 40.38 (single consumer GPT-OSS 20B, one seed).
limits: Oracle numbers are single seed, one model. Exact matches excluded from the main corpus to avoid leakage.
agent_relevance: Memory transfers across task types; near-duplicate leakage inflates results, so audit any memory benchmark for it.

source: Kim et al. (2026) Multi-Agent Transactive Memory: scaling, capability gap, cost
finding: Benefit grew with index size on ALFWorld. On WebArena success dipped at 50% index then reached 20.9% at full size. Weaker and stronger producers helped consumers alike. Producer capability gap did not predict gain.
numbers: Correlation of capability gap with retrieval advantage: r=+0.04 (p=0.49) ALFWorld single-stage; r=+0.09 (p=0.09) with SVMRank; r=+0.03 (p=0.79) and +0.08 (p=0.35) WebArena. Tokens per successful episode fell 10.7-34.2% in the single-stage runs for the setting rows read, but total input tokens rose in most settings.
limits: Non-monotonic WebArena curve explained only by hypothesis. Cost result mixed by setting.
agent_relevance: Credibility of a source (a core TMS dimension) was not predicted by source model strength here: do not rank memory sources by assumed expertise alone.

source: Kim et al. (2026) Multi-Agent Transactive Memory: retrieval planner
finding: Each consumer has a RetrievalPlanner LLM that decides per step whether to query the shared memory. Authors say indiscriminate retrieval dilutes context.
numbers: Window l=5 steps; retrieval budget of one chunk per call. No separate on/off ablation number found in the text read.
limits: The dilution claim is stated, not measured here.
agent_relevance: A gate that decides when to consult memory is a code-level operator we can copy: retrieval is a decision, not a default.

source: Li, Naito, Shirado (2026, ICML) Systematic Failures in Collective Reasoning under Distributed Information (HiddenBench)
finding: Hidden-profile paradigm (Stasser and Titus 1985) run on LLM agents: 65 tasks, 15 frontier models. Groups fail to surface unshared facts and converge early on shared evidence.
numbers: Multi-agent accuracy 30.1% with distributed info vs 80.7% for single agents with full info. Humans on same tasks: pre-discussion 0.125, post 0.385, full-profile 0.604 (p=0.003 post vs full). GPT-4.1 agents: pre 0.008, post 0.233, full 0.733 (p<0.001 for the pre-to-post rise).
limits: Task set auto-generated: 57 of 200 candidates passed validation (28.5%). Group-size and round effects measured mostly on GPT-4.1.
agent_relevance: Cleanest LLM test of the reason TMS exists. A single agent given everything beats a group that must pool. Our one-agent design avoids the pooling failure only if all facts are put in one context.

source: Li, Naito, Shirado (2026, ICML) Systematic Failures in Collective Reasoning under Distributed Information (HiddenBench): prompting
finding: No prompt style closed the gap. Telling agents the information is asymmetric helped some. Telling them to share everything helped most but left half the gap.
numbers: GPT-4.1 post-discussion accuracy: cooperative 0.200-0.242, conflictual: zero majority consensus, zero-shot CoT about 0.222, informing asymmetry about 0.367, share-all 0.467, versus 0.233 default and 0.733 full profile (table columns read from text layout; CoT and asymmetry values are my reading).
limits: One model for the prompt table; averages from small run counts.
agent_relevance: Prompts like 'think step by step' did nothing for pooling. A procedure (who states what) is needed, not a style cue.

source: Li, Naito, Shirado (2026, ICML) Systematic Failures in Collective Reasoning under Distributed Information (HiddenBench): rounds and group size
finding: More discussion and more agents made pooling worse or flat. Extended discussion reinforces consensus on shared facts.
numbers: Rounds T=5/10/15/20: peak at 15 (0.233), decline at 20. Group size N=3 to 7: gain from communication drops from +0.348 to +0.006.
limits: GPT-4.1 only for these sweeps; new tasks generated for N above 4.
agent_relevance: Adding more agents is not a fix. Mirrors the human finding that bigger groups share fewer unique facts.

source: Li, Naito, Shirado (2026, ICML) Systematic Failures in Collective Reasoning under Distributed Information (HiddenBench): isolating the bottleneck and structured protocol
finding: Forcing every agent to reveal all facts nearly fixes accuracy, so the fault is surfacing, not reasoning. A secretary summarizer helps little. A two-stage Exchange-then-Decide protocol lifts accuracy a lot.
numbers: 18 tasks. Baseline vs Reveal-All: GPT-4.1 0.037 to 0.926; Gemini-2.5-Flash 0.173 to 0.982. Secretary: 0.241 and 0.713. Structured protocol (2 exchange rounds: each agent states 1-2 facts plus one reason the front-runner may be wrong; then one decide pass): GPT-4.1 0.037 to 0.800, Gemini-2.5-Flash 0.173 to 0.727, Flash-Lite 0.043 to 0.743.
limits: 18 tasks, 5 runs each, 4 agents; protocol designed on the same benchmark family.
agent_relevance: A fixed 'state your unique facts plus one counter-reason' step is a cheap scaffold. Maps to a directory-building step: ask each source what only it knows.

source: Li, Naito, Shirado (2026, ICML) Systematic Failures in Collective Reasoning under Distributed Information (HiddenBench): structured dissent
finding: One adversarial agent out of four helped GPT-4.1 but hurt Gemini-2.5-Flash. No dissent level helped all models.
numbers: GPT-4.1 0.233 to 0.492 with 25% dissent. Gemini-2.5-Flash 0.889 without dissent, 0.306 with one adversary.
limits: Heterogeneity alone did not close the gap to full profile.
agent_relevance: Forced dissent is model-dependent; test per model before making it a guardrail.

source: Babu et al. (2026) Consilience: Conformally Calibrated Communication Control for Hidden-Profile Multi-Agent Reasoning
finding: A controller reads a compact discussion state (uncertainty, disagreement, evidence gain, redundancy, premature consensus) and picks challenge, clarify, seek-evidence or route to a chosen speaker. Conformal calibration bounds one-step regret.
numbers: HiddenBench, 12 models: best controller 0.83 vs 0.26 for fixed round-robin (+0.57); reaches or beats full-information on 11 of 12 models, mean +0.13. Across 15 models: hidden pre 0.083, round-robin 0.285, full info 0.731; Rules controller 0.843, LLM 0.816, LLM+Vote 0.815, MLP 0.785.
limits: Preprint; benchmark is the family the controller was built on; held-out MLP 0.73 vs in-domain 0.77. Smallest Qwen3 models gained little. Baselines are reproduced from the HiddenBench paper.
agent_relevance: A program-side controller choosing the next speaker or question matches our schema (program decides, model fills a slot). The rule-based controller won, so no learning is needed.

source: Babu et al. (2026) Consilience: Conformally Calibrated Communication Control for Hidden-Profile Multi-Agent Reasoning: ablations
finding: Removing the route action (engaging underrepresented agents) hurt most; removing seek-new-evidence also hurt. Some action removals improved results. Belief-only state features gave shortest talks but lowest accuracy.
numbers: State-feature ablation: full state 82.22% success; belief+information 77.78%; belief+cost 77.78%; belief-only 75.56%. Qwen3-8B, 400 trials: LLM and MLP controllers 82.75%.
limits: Small ablation counts; actions interact.
agent_relevance: Routing the question to whoever has not spoken is the 'retrieval by directory' step. It was the most valuable single action.

source: Li et al. (2023) Theory of Mind for Multi-Agent Collaboration via Large Language Models
finding: LLM teams in a cooperative text game (bomb defusal, 3 agents) show emergent collaboration. Failures come from long-horizon context and hallucinated task state. An explicit written belief state fixes much of it and raises ToM inference accuracy.
numbers: Score: ChatGPT 43.3; GPT-4 90; GPT-4+belief 90. Rounds to finish: GPT-4 28.3, GPT-4+belief 12.3, MAPPO 11.0, CBS planner 6.0. Valid action rate 62.5% / 71.8% / 86.1% (ChatGPT / GPT-4 / GPT-4+belief; column order as extracted). ToM accuracy ChatGPT / GPT-4 / GPT-4+belief: introspection 79.0/80.0/97.2; first-order 41.9/60.0/80.1; second-order 11.6/64.3/69.4.
limits: Human annotators with a global view produced ground truth; belief state covers own beliefs, not teammates'.
agent_relevance: Closest older machine analogue of 'who knows what': tracking what a teammate knows. A written belief state about others is a testable memory slot.

source: Hu, Stegner, Mutlu (2023) Knowing Who Knows What: Designing Socially Assistive Robots with Transactive Memory System
finding: Position paper. Maps Wegner's three stages (encoding, storage, retrieval) onto a robot that learns what each group member knows and redirects people to the right expert. No experiment.
numbers: No data. Design opportunities listed per stage; example of a robot remembering a nearby therapist.
limits: Workshop paper (CHI 2023); untested concept.
agent_relevance: Gives a clean three-stage template (record who knows what; store; route queries) for any agent that consults several sources.

source: Meske, Hermanns, Brachten (2026) The GenAI Who Knew Too Little: Revisiting Transactive Memory Systems in Human GenAI Collaboration
finding: Interviews with knowledge workers: humans learn what the AI is good at, but the AI holds only temporary, in-session knowledge of the human. Trust is ambivalent: they credit expertise yet verify. Flow is top-down, AI lacks initiative.
numbers: 14 interviews, 19-89 min (mean 29); 11 used GenAI daily or almost daily. Three TMS dimensions: specialization asymmetric, credibility ambivalent, coordination hierarchical.
limits: N=14, self-report, GenAI-familiar sample; qualitative only.
agent_relevance: Authors say the AI lacks metamemory and persistent memory of the user. A scaffold can add both: persist a source directory and a confidence record.

source: Islam, Akgun, Billah (2026) Shaping Credibility Judgments in Human-GenAI Partnership via Weaker LLMs
finding: Randomised classroom study using a small local LLM (Qwen 2.5 7B). Making students think first lowered over-trust in the AI. Specialization and coordination scores did not change.
numbers: N=42, three arms of 12-18. Mid-semester ANCOVA F(2,38)=4.02, p=.026, partial eta2=.175. Post F(2,38)=5.48, p=.008, partial eta2=.224. Adjusted means: reflection-first 5.65, verification-required 6.22, control 6.60; only reflection-first vs control significant (Holm p=.006).
limits: Small N, one course, survey measure, single weaker model.
agent_relevance: Order matters: answer first, then consult the source. Same shape as 'form own answer before reading retrieved memory' to cut anchoring.

source: Akgun and Toker (2026) When Does GenAI Use Support Critical Thinking? A Cross-Cultural Structural Account of Transactive Memory with GenAI
finding: Structural model: critical thinking came from dividing and coordinating labor with the AI and from reworking its output. Confidence and self-rated ability had no direct effect.
numbers: 891 students, US and Turkiye. Baseline fit chi2(8)=24.258, CFI=.974, RMSEA=.048. Indirect via specialization-and-coordination .147 (p=.002), via reflective transformation .064 (p=.009), total .211 (p<.001). Confidence-by-ability interaction -0.104; low-ability simple slope .238 (p<.001), high .042 (n.s.). Partial invariance needed (2 paths freed).
limits: Cross-sectional; binary outcome; smaller Turkish sample; self-report; cultural explanations not directly tested.
agent_relevance: Supports 'rework the output' as the active ingredient, not mere use. Matches our guardrail that the model never accepts its own text without a check.

source: Annunziata et al. (2026) When AI Joins the Team! A Model of How AI Adoption Relates to Social Patterns in Software Engineering Teams
finding: TMS-based instruments for human-AI and human-human work in software teams. AI use links to more peer knowledge sharing in specialization work and better communication quality in coordination work; mediation mostly not significant.
numbers: PLS-SEM, N=152 professionals. H_AI_Spec to HH_Spec beta=.253 (p=.005, f2=.069). Indirect on knowledge fragmentation beta=-.059 (p=.121, n.s.); on expertise misalignment -.061 (p=.074). Communication-fragmentation indirect .045 (p=.494), unhealthy-interaction -.011 (p=.738). Some AVE values about .45, just under .50.
limits: Cross-sectional survey; low R2; some construct validity marginal.
agent_relevance: AI complemented human sharing rather than replacing it. Weak support for any claim that an AI memory partner reduces siloing.

source: Liu et al. (2024) iAgents: Autonomous Agents for Collaborative Task under Information Asymmetry
finding: Each human gets an agent holding that human's private data. Agents message each other to fill missing facts. InfoNav keeps an explicit plan of which facts are still missing; a mixed fuzzy-plus-clear memory supplies retrieval.
numbers: InformativeBench average accuracy 50.48% with strong backbones; hardest task 22.8%. Social network of 140 people and 588 relations. Without InfoNav no Schedule level exceeded 10% accuracy; InfoNav added 15-26% on NP and Schedule. Mixed memory +2.38 to +6.34% and recursive communication +12.7% on FriendsTV.
limits: Own benchmark; most smaller models near 50% on the easiest task and under 20% on the hardest Schedule items. First-author name not read from page; check before citing.
agent_relevance: The InfoNav plan is a 'what do I still need and who has it' ledger. A tested TMS-like directory step with large measured effect.

source: INMS: Memory Sharing for Large Language Model based Agents (2024, v-later revision)
finding: A shared pool of prompt-answer pairs written by several agents, with an adaptive retriever. Every agent improved against no sharing, even with memories from different backbones.
numbers: Three domains (literary creation, unconventional logic, plan generation), nine agents, 1000 items; 3 shared memories at test, gpt-4o backbone. Beat BM25, random and dense baselines on F1 and LLM-judge scores. Exact deltas are in tables not extracted.
limits: Open-ended tasks scored by BertScore and LLM judge; tables not read in full so effect sizes are not recorded.
agent_relevance: Shows heterogeneous-model memory sharing works; authors seeded an echo-chamber test on purpose, so sharing can also spread errors.

source: Collaborative Memory: Multi-User Memory Sharing in LLM Agents with Dynamic Access Control (2025)
finding: Two memory tiers (private, shared) with provenance on each fragment and permission-based read and write policies. Sharing cut repeated tool calls and kept accuracy.
numbers: MultiHop-RAG (609 articles, 2,556 questions), five users: accuracy above 0.90 on average with collaboration, slightly lower isolated; resource use down by up to 61% at 50% query overlap and 59% at 75% overlap. Asymmetric scenario had no ground truth, so only usage measured.
limits: Simulated users. Scenario 2 has no accuracy data. Authors not read from page; check before citing.
agent_relevance: Provenance on every memory item plus access rules is the credibility and permission part of a TMS. Cheap to adopt.

source: Chang (2025) AGI Requires a Coordination Layer on Top of Pattern Repositories (MACI)
finding: Uses 'transactional memory' (SagaLLM-style checkpoint and rollback of commitments) as the persistence layer of a multi-agent stack. This is software transactions, not Wegner's transactive memory, so the name collides.
numbers: Reports sycophancy failures 11.4% reduced to 0.0% with PID-style debate control; GPT-4-Turbo 75% vs GPT-5.2 20% L3 safety on one counterfactual benchmark. Nothing isolates the memory component.
limits: Single-group programme paper; claims for the memory layer are not isolated. The label mismatch is the main warning.
agent_relevance: Search carefully: 'transactional memory' hits are mostly hardware or database transactions. Only the commitment-ledger idea transfers.

source: Chen et al. (2026, CHI) Through the Lens of Human-Human Collaboration: A Configurable Research Platform for Exploring Human-Agent Collaboration
finding: Platform that runs classic CSCW tasks with humans and LLM agents, including Hidden Profile variants. A case study shows agents react to workspace awareness differently from humans.
numbers: Awareness study: human wealth $375.1 vs $376.6 across conditions; agent wealth fell from $254.0 to $218.1 when the dashboard was removed. 16 human participants; one human plus five agents per session.
limits: Tiny N; Shape Factory is not a TMS test; hidden-profile data not reported in the part read.
agent_relevance: LLM agents seem to depend on a shared status board (who holds what) more than humans do: a visible directory is useful for models.

source: Lu, Yuan, McLeod (2012) Twenty-five years of hidden profiles in group decision making: a meta-analysis (as cited by HiddenBench and Consilience)
finding: Cited by both LLM papers: groups discuss more common than unique information and are much less likely to find the right answer under hidden than full information.
numbers: Numbers not read in this session; see angle A/B files.
limits: Second-hand through the two LLM papers.
agent_relevance: Human baseline that the LLM results echo; the LLM gap (30.1 vs 80.7) is of the same kind.

source: Stasser and Titus (1985) Pooling of unshared information in group decision making (as cited by HiddenBench)
finding: Founding hidden-profile study; HiddenBench adapts its scenario materials.
numbers: Not opened; see angle A.
limits: Second-hand.
agent_relevance: Origin of the paradigm used to test LLM groups.

source: Wegner (1987) Transactive memory: a contemporary analysis of the group mind (as cited by Kim et al., Meske et al., Hu et al.)
finding: All machine papers read cite Wegner for the 'who knows what' directory plus encoding, storage and retrieval. Only Meske et al., Islam et al., Akgun and Toker, and Annunziata et al. use the Lewis-style specialization, credibility, coordination dimensions, all in human-AI surveys or interviews.
numbers: Not opened here.
limits: Second-hand.
agent_relevance: The machine literature mostly imports the label; no study found tests a Wegner-style expertise directory inside an LLM agent loop with a measured ablation, except iAgents' InfoNav plan and Consilience's route action, which are close analogues.
